extracted.intended_audience: European patent attorneys, EPO/UPC practitioners, patent prosecutors and oppositions counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and legal guidance on interpreting patent claims under the EPC after the EBA decision G 1/24, with implications for prosecution, opposition, added‑matter and claim/draft strategy before the EPO and UPC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims are the starting point and basis for patentability assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: “The claims are the starting point and the basis for assessing the patentability of an invention under Articles 52 to 57 EPC.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boards of Appeal consistently start from the claims as the basis for patentability assessment. Interpretation begins from the claims, but other sources (see below) will be consulted in that process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description and drawings shall always be consulted to interpret claims for patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: “The description and drawings shall always be consulted to interpret the claims when assessing the patentability of an invention under Articles 52 to 57 EPC, and not only if the person skilled in the art finds a claim to be unclear or ambiguous when read in isolation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing novelty and inventive step, examiners and parties must take the entire disclosure into account. This departs from a practice that consulted the description only when a claim appeared ambiguous in isolation. The decision aligns EPO practice with national courts and the UPC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 69 and Article 84 may be applied analogously for patentability purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: The EBA notes that neither Article 69 nor Article 84 EPC provides a fully satisfactory legal basis for interpreting patent claims during patentability assessment, and that the strictly formal answer to whether Article 69(1), second sentence, and Article 1 of the Protocol apply for patentability would be “No”. However, existing case law applies these provisions analogously to patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners may rely on Art.69/Protocol and Art.84 reasoning analogously when arguing interpretation for novelty/inventive step, even though Art.69 is primarily about infringement and Art.84 concerns clarity/formal requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: A finding of clarity is itself an act of interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The EBA states that the finding that a claim is clear is in itself an act of interpretation, i.e. the conclusion that a claim is clear cannot be reached without having interpreted the subject-matter of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One cannot avoid interpretation by claiming that a claim is ‘clear on its face’; reaching clarity requires interpretive steps and therefore consultation of the description/drawings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct response to any unclarity in a claim is amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: EBA: “The correct response to any unclarity in a claim is amendment.” (Reasons 20)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners are likely to request claim amendments for clarity under Article 84 EPC. Applicants should be prepared to amend claims to remove unclarity, but must balance this against added‑matter constraints (see related rubric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Any amendment must be directly and unambiguously derivable from the original application and must not result in an intermediate generalisation
rubrics_metrics.description: According to EPO case law and Guidelines, any amendment must be “directly and unambiguously” derivable from the original application and must not result in an “intermediate generalisation”.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive reliance on Article 84 to force extensive amendments can undermine substantive quality because permissible amendments are tightly constrained. When responding to clarity objections, ensure that proposed amendments meet Art.123(2) standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft claims with EPO‑proven language and provide fallback positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants should draft their applications with claim language that is – as far as possible – “EPO‑proven” to ensure clarity from the outset. Broad claims should always be accompanied by proper fallback positions, either within the claims themselves or in a general part of the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic drafting reduces the risk that later clarity requests force claim narrowing that cannot be supported by original disclosure, avoiding an “inescapable trap” between clarity and original‑disclosure requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful when adapting the description to the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Now that it is certain that the description will also be taken into account when interpreting the claims in potential opposition proceedings, particular care must be taken when adapting the description to the claims during examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any addition or deletion to or from the description should be carefully assessed for its implications on claim interpretation. An apparently simple adaptation can change the meaning of a claim term and open attacks for alleged added matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation‑first approach can assist patentees defending added‑matter attacks
rubrics_metrics.description: If, for questions of added matter under Art. 123(2) EPC or Art. 100(c) EPC, these provisions require that the subject‑matter be determined, the patent claims must be interpreted consistently with Articles 52 to 57 EPC, i.e., in the light of the description and figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In opposition, patentees may invoke interpretation in light of the description to argue that a term added to a claim is synonymous with wording in the original disclosure; if adhered to, this may reduce findings of inadmissible extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioners must be familiar with both EPO and UPC case law
rubrics_metrics.description: The EBA explicitly aligns itself with the UPC and stresses the need for consistent interpretation of Article 69 EPC across jurisdictions. Practitioners should ensure that they are well‑versed in and able to apply the case law of both the EBA and the UPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the EBA referenced UPC decisions (e.g., 10x Genomics v. Nanostring) and harmonisation is a stated goal, counsel must track and apply jurisprudence from both forums when formulating interpretation and amendment arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: No detailed method mandated for how to use the description; spectrum of approaches possible
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision states the proposition that the description and drawings shall always be consulted for interpretation, but does not give guidance on how claim interpretation should be conducted on this basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible approaches range from a minimalistic position (consider only explicit definitions in the description) to broader functional/systematic approaches giving less weight to claim wording. Near term, EPO practice is expected to be limited to considering definitions or other unambiguous statements in the description, though the existing body of case law may require deeper interpretation in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical expectations in prosecution: examiners’ time constraints and tactical opportunities for applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the limited amount of time examiners have to prepare reports, it is unlikely that EPO search and examination reports will routinely prioritize claim interpretation up front. However, the decision gives applicants a legal basis for opening such discussions if helpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants can proactively request interpretation discussions; but expect examiners to be more inclined to require clarity amendments rather than undertake extended interpretative analysis due to resource constraints.
